records.title: unit overview
records.heading: unit overview
records.body: the akron general neuroscience icu is a fully operational 10-bed neuro icu within a comprehensive stroke center and a level i trauma center. the unit provides multidisciplinary, evidence-based care for patients with complex neurological and neurosurgical conditions, including acute stroke, traumatic brain injury, intracranial hemorrhage, status epilepticus, spinal cord injury, and other critical neurologic illnesses.

records.title: part 2 · scope of practice & admissions
records.heading: part 2 · scope of practice & admissions
records.body: navigation cue: use this section for admission ownership, trauma boundaries, and who is primary versus consulting. return to start here. the neuroscience icu (nsicu) team provides comprehensive critical care management for patients with neurological and neurosurgical conditions admitted to the nsicu.

records.title: primary admission responsibilities
records.heading: primary admission responsibilities
records.body: the nsicu team serves as the primary admitting service for patients with: acute ischemic stroke intracerebral hemorrhage (ich) subarachnoid hemorrhage (sah) other neurological and neurosurgical critical illnesses key point · patients with non-traumatic intracranial hemorrhage are routinely admitted to the nsicu for the initial 24 hours of intensive monitoring. ongoing disposition is determined by the patient's clinical condition and level of care required.

records.title: isolated traumatic brain injury (tbi)
records.heading: isolated traumatic brain injury (tbi)
records.body: patients with isolated moderate-to-severe tbi are admitted under the trauma surgery service. the nsicu team provides all neurocritical care management in collaboration with the trauma surgery and neurosurgery teams. following completion of the tertiary trauma survey and clearance by the trauma service, primary responsibility for patient management is transferred to the nsicu team.

records.title: polytrauma patients
records.heading: polytrauma patients
records.body: patients with multiple traumatic injuries remain under the trauma surgery/surgical icu (sicu) service. the nsicu team functions as a consulting service, providing specialized neurocritical care recommendations while the trauma/sicu team maintains primary responsibility.

records.title: tracheostomy & peg placement
records.heading: tracheostomy & peg placement
records.body: for patients admitted to the nsicu who require tracheostomy and/or percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (peg) placement, these procedures are performed by the trauma/sicu team.

records.title: critical care consultation for trauma patients
records.heading: critical care consultation for trauma patients
records.body: the trauma surgery/sicu team should be contacted first for icu consultation. if both teams determine that additional expertise is required, a medical icu (micu) consultation may then be requested. avoid requesting a primary micu consultation before discussing the case with the trauma/sicu team. interdisciplinary communication · management decisions involving multiple services should be based on direct attending-to-attending communication. early collaboration between the nsicu, trauma surgery, neurosurgery, and other consulting services is strongly encouraged to ensure coordinated patient care and timely resolution of management issues.

records.title: part 3 · daily workflow & expectations
records.heading: part 3 · daily workflow & expectations
records.body: navigation cue: use this section during the day to confirm rounds, airway coverage, and required icu checklist habits. return to start here.

records.title: the daily rhythm
records.heading: the daily rhythm
records.body: time activity details 7:00 am arrival & handoff faculty are expected to arrive by 7:00 am to receive handoff and prepare for morning rounds. 8:45 am (m-f) multidisciplinary discharge planning rounds all nsicu providers attend whenever clinical responsibilities permit. 9:00 am daily nsicu interdisciplinary bedside rounds led by the bedside nurse using a system-based approach. 7 am - 5 pm nsicu attending covers airway & emergencies includes code blue events for nsicu patients. after 5 pm micu covers airway & emergency response micu remains available for emergency consultation and critical care assistance.

records.title: airway & emergency response
records.heading: airway & emergency response
records.body: the nsicu attending is responsible for airway management for patients admitted under the nsicu service between 7:00 am and 5:00 pm. the nsicu team responds to medical emergencies and code blue events involving nsicu patients. nsicu advanced practice providers (apps) do not perform endotracheal intubation; airway management is the responsibility of the attending physician. after 5:00 pm, the micu team provides airway management and emergency response support for nsicu patients.

records.title: 8:45 am - multidisciplinary discharge planning rounds
records.heading: 8:45 am - multidisciplinary discharge planning rounds
records.body: primary objectives: review each patient's overall clinical status and anticipated discharge needs. discuss barriers to discharge and care transitions. review the ongoing need for invasive lines and devices (e.g., central venous catheters, arterial lines, foley catheters) and place removal orders when appropriate. coordinate rehabilitation and post-acute care planning. the multidisciplinary team includes care management, bedside nursing, physical therapy (pt), occupational therapy (ot), speech-language pathology (slp), and additional disciplines as needed. these collaborative rounds facilitate early discharge planning and ensure coordinated, patient-centered stroke and neurocritical care.

records.title: 9:00 am - nsicu interdisciplinary bedside rounds
records.heading: 9:00 am - nsicu interdisciplinary bedside rounds
records.body: the bedside nurse presents the patient's current clinical status using a structured systems assessment. the multidisciplinary team develops and reviews the daily plan of care. patients and family members are encouraged to participate in bedside rounds whenever appropriate. icu checklist - required every patient, every day · a standardized icu checklist must be completed for every patient during rounds. the checklist incorporates sccm best practices, including the abcdef bundle, and is available within epic. routine review ensures consistent implementation of evidence-based practices: pain management, sedation optimization, delirium prevention, early mobility, spontaneous awakening and breathing trials, family engagement, and line/device stewardship. · the checklist is part of the progress note. staff can add it to their attestation with the smartphrase .icuchecklistreport

records.title: part 4 · consultation & stroke alerts
records.heading: part 4 · consultation & stroke alerts
records.body: navigation cue: use this section when a neurologic consult or stroke alert question comes up. return to start here.

records.title: inpatient neurology support
records.heading: inpatient neurology support
records.body: all patients admitted to the nsicu with acute ischemic stroke, intracerebral hemorrhage, or other complex neurological disorders should receive a neurology consultation. inpatient neurology provides consultation for cerebrovascular patients and collaborates closely with the nsicu team regarding diagnosis, medical management, secondary prevention, and disposition. at akron general, neurology functions as a consulting service only and does not serve as the admitting team.

records.title: neurocritical care consultation
records.heading: neurocritical care consultation
records.body: the nsicu service provides neurocritical care consultations for non-stroke patients admitted to other icus when appropriate. if the nsicu attending is not a neurologist, non-stroke neurological consultations are provided by the general neurology service. the icu team can ask neurology to evaluate further if needs are complex. hospital-wide stroke consultations, including icu patients, are managed by the stroke neurology team. always the nsicu team's responsibility · regardless of attending background, the nsicu team is responsible for: · cardiac arrest prognostication · liver failure with cerebral edema · brain death evaluation

records.title: stroke alert process
records.heading: stroke alert process
records.body: suspected acute stroke · any patient with suspected acute stroke: activate a stroke alert immediately. the stroke neurology team is responsible for responding to all stroke alerts. their responsibilities include: rapid neurological evaluation eligibility assessment for thrombolytic therapy (tnk) coordination of endovascular thrombectomy evaluation with the neuroendovascular team ongoing acute stroke management recommendations note · the nsicu team does not respond to hospital stroke alerts unless specifically requested for consultation or patient transfer.

records.title: part 5 · emergency transfers & ecmo
records.heading: part 5 · emergency transfers & ecmo
records.body: navigation cue: use this section for cct, auto launch, emergency transfers, and ecmo escalation. return to start here.

records.title: auto launch & the cct process
records.heading: auto launch & the cct process
records.body: transfer line: 216-448-7000 (cleveland clinic critical care transport dispatch) at cleveland clinic, the auto launch process is an expedited emergency transfer protocol. it quickly transports patients with life-threatening conditions (such as heart attacks or strokes) from regional hospitals to definitive care.

records.title: acute stroke / ich transfer workflow
records.heading: acute stroke / ich transfer workflow
records.body: step what happens 1. trigger a referring hospital identifies a patient with acute ischemic stroke, ich, sah, large vessel occlusion (lvo), or another time-sensitive neurological emergency requiring a higher level of care. 2. the call the referring physician contacts the cleveland clinic critical care transport (cct) dispatch center through the dedicated transfer line to initiate an emergency transfer. 3. transport activation following acceptance by the receiving physician, cct immediately dispatches the most appropriate resource (helicopter, fixed-wing, or mobile icu ambulance). transport begins while the receiving team coordinates bed placement. 4. pre-arrival coordination neurocritical care, stroke neurology, neurosurgery, and/or neuroendovascular teams are notified per diagnosis. brain imaging is electronically transferred and reviewed when available. treatment plans (thrombolysis, thrombectomy, neurosurgical intervention, neurocritical care) are developed before arrival. the receiving icu, angio suite, or, or ed is prepared. communication is facilitated by epic secure chat, ccf iphone messaging, and direct phone calls. 5. direct handoff on arrival the patient goes directly to the appropriate destination: neuro icu, microangiography suite (mechanical thrombectomy), or, or ed (if additional stabilization is needed). a structured physician-to-physician and nurse-to-nurse handoff ensures continuity and timely definitive treatment. guiding principle - time is brain · early activation of transport, multidisciplinary communication, and parallel preparation of the receiving team are essential to minimize treatment delays and optimize neurological outcomes.

records.title: diagnoses eligible for emergency transfer (incl. auto launch)
records.heading: diagnoses eligible for emergency transfer (incl. auto launch)
records.body: acute ischemic stroke within the treatment window for thrombolysis and/or mechanical thrombectomy intracerebral hemorrhage (ich) subarachnoid hemorrhage (sah) cerebral edema with impending or established brain herniation status epilepticus or refractory seizures moderate-to-severe traumatic brain injury (tbi) acute hydrocephalus spinal cord compression or other neurosurgical emergencies any rapidly deteriorating neurological condition requiring emergent neurocritical care at the discretion of the receiving neuro icu physician or the referring physician, an auto-launch of cct may be initiated for patients requiring emergent neurocritical care, allowing transport to begin while the receiving team coordinates definitive care. the cct team coordinates all aspects of the transfer and provides clinical guidance to the referring team for stabilization before and during transport; when additional neurocritical care expertise is needed, cct may contact the nsicu physician to facilitate transfer and provide management recommendations.

records.title: 1. trigger: suspected need for ecmo
records.heading: 1. trigger: suspected need for ecmo
records.body: consider ecmo activation in patients with severe cardiopulmonary failure, including: cardiac arrest, refractory shock, ards, massive pulmonary embolism (pe), cardiogenic shock, or severe shock unresponsive to standard therapy.

records.title: 2. immediate actions
records.heading: 2. immediate actions
records.body: stat consults: medical icu (330-250-1634) and cardiothoracic surgery (per qgenda on-call schedule). early physician-to-physician communication may be required to determine candidacy and coordinate care. resuscitation: continue aggressive resuscitation as clinically indicated. initial workup: abg, serum lactate, stat bedside echocardiogram (micu), consider pa catheter if indicated, portable ct brain if clinically appropriate.

records.title: ecmo candidacy assessment
records.heading: ecmo candidacy assessment
records.body: multidisciplinary evaluation by micu, ct surgery, and the primary team to assess inclusion and exclusion criteria. nsicu involvement for assessment of neurologic status and anticoagulation contraindications as needed. coordination with neurosurgery and/or vascular neurology when anticoagulation risk is present. clear documentation of risk-benefit discussion in patients with high bleeding risk.

records.title: pulmonary embolism pathway
records.heading: pulmonary embolism pathway
records.body: stat micu consultation for consideration of systemic thrombolysis, catheter-directed thrombectomy, or ecmo support when indicated.

records.title: 3. ecmo team activation
records.heading: 3. ecmo team activation
records.body: notify the on-call micu attending (akron) immediately. call the transfer center (216-448-7000) and request activation of: 2shock team, j31 ecmo fellow, and critical care transport (cct).

records.title: 4. decision point: on-site ecmo deployment
records.heading: 4. decision point: on-site ecmo deployment
records.body: if ecmo is initiated on-site: cardiothoracic surgery proceeds with cannulation (bedside or cath lab depending on hemodynamic stability). coordinate with cct/transfer center to ensure perfusion support for transport. determine cannulation location based on clinical stability and urgency. if ecmo is not initiated on-site: stabilize the patient and arrange transfer to a higher level of care facility as appropriate.

records.title: 5. escalation contact
records.heading: 5. escalation contact
records.body: ecmo lead: dr. lokesh venkat - 216-212-6977 key principle · early recognition of ecmo candidacy and rapid multidisciplinary activation are critical to improving outcomes in severe cardiopulmonary failure.

records.title: part 6 · documentation & quality
records.heading: part 6 · documentation & quality
records.body: navigation cue: use this section for stroke metrics, epic pathway requirements, consent, poa variables, billing, and cdi. return to start here. why this matters · all patients admitted for acute ischemic stroke, ich, or sah must be managed using the standardized stroke care pathway in epic. complete, accurate documentation supports: · comprehensive stroke center certification · cleveland clinic quality metrics and regulatory compliance · performance improvement initiatives · optimal patient care and multidisciplinary communication

records.heading: required clinical documentation (every eligible patient)
records.body: element detail last known well (lkw) date and time arrival date and time of arrival to the treating facility stroke diagnosis/type acute ischemic stroke; ich; sah; sdh when applicable nihss nih stroke scale - documented time must match the key metrics section mrs modified rankin scale (pre-stroke baseline and discharge, when applicable) gcs glasgow coma scale ct / cta findings including identification of large vessel occlusion when present tnk/alteplase eligibility including inclusion and exclusion criteria thrombectomy eligibility and documentation of endovascular treatment decisions

records.heading: hemorrhagic stroke severity scores

records.title: consent & code status (icu admission)
records.heading: consent & code status (icu admission)
records.body: consent and code status for all icu-level procedures should be confirmed and documented immediately upon patient arrival. code status at admission · code status must be clearly recorded in the medical record at the time of admission - it is a critical determinant of outcomes and quality metrics. patients documented as dnr on admission, based on prior expressed wishes or advance directives, should be classified as present on admission (poa). accurate, timely documentation is vital for patient safety, alignment with goals of care, and institutional mortality and quality reporting. icu consent (smartphrase: .nicuconsent) the app is not credentialed for independent airway management; therefore, informed consent for icu-level procedures should be obtained upon admission whenever feasible. icu consent includes authorization for routine critical care interventions, including but not limited to: endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation central venous catheter placement arterial line placement blood product transfusion pulmonary artery catheter insertion bronchoscopy and related diagnostic/therapeutic procedures lumbar puncture (lp) these procedures are considered part of standard icu care and may be performed as clinically indicated.

records.title: procedure-specific consent requirements
records.heading: procedure-specific consent requirements
records.body: in addition to standard icu consent, separate informed consent must be obtained for non-routine or procedure-specific interventions. these are not covered under general icu admission consent and require individual documentation: paracentesis thoracentesis chest tube insertion any other invasive or procedural intervention not explicitly included under routine icu care each procedure must have its own dedicated consent form or documentation prior to performance, unless an emergency exception applies where delay would pose immediate risk to life or limb.

records.heading: progress notes & h&p

records.title: part 7 · transitions of care
records.heading: part 7 · transitions of care
records.body: navigation cue: use this section when deciding pcu/floor readiness or preparing an icu transfer note. return to start here. the nsicu team is responsible for coordinating safe and appropriate transfer of patients out of the icu to the next level of care.

records.title: who transfers whom
records.heading: who transfers whom
records.body: patient population disposition pathway nsicu primary patients discharged directly from the nsicu team to the appropriate destination (step-down unit, floor, long-term care, or acute rehabilitation facility). trauma patients (nsicu providing critical care) remain primarily under trauma oversight for disposition decisions. transitions to ltac or acute rehab are coordinated by the nsicu team in collaboration with trauma surgery. non-surgical tbi patients stable for the floor transition to trauma surgery or sound hospital medicine based on clinical needs and service alignment. neurosurgical (primary tbi) patients patients who undergo neurosurgical intervention are generally managed and discharged under the neurosurgery (nsgy) service. complex medical needs may require multidisciplinary discussion (trauma, nsgy, nsicu, medicine) to determine disposition. floor transfers nsicu patients requiring ongoing inpatient floor care are transferred to sound hospital medicine (pager 330-250-1576) or family medicine (for established cfm patients). if transfer barriers arise · effective physician-to-physician and team-to-team communication is essential for safe, timely transfer. if disagreements or barriers cannot be resolved through direct communication between services, escalate to the unit medical director and trauma service leadership.

records.title: level-of-care criteria
records.heading: level-of-care criteria
records.body: each patient remains under the care of their primary icu service. neurocritical care and neurosurgical patients are continuously managed by the nsicu team throughout their icu admission. intensive care (icu) intermediate care (pcu) general medical floor new, unstable stroke requiring neuro checks q1h or more frequent and/or life support therapies. acute stroke receiving thrombolytics or neurovascular interventional procedures. established, stable stroke requiring frequent neuro checks q2-3h, or frequent suctioning/turning q2-3h. stable stroke requiring neuro checks, suctioning, or turning q4h or less frequent. unstable severe tbi requiring life support therapies. stable severe tbi requiring frequent positioning and q2h neuro checks; minimal respiratory issues including suction needs. stable post-severe tbi requiring neuro checks, suctioning, or turning q4h or less frequent. unstable sah requiring life support therapies. sah post-aneurysm clipping requiring observation for vasospasm or hydrocephalus. sah post-aneurysm treatment requiring observation and neurovascular checks more frequently than q4h, without major evidence of vasospasm or electrolyte disturbance. no signs of vasospasm or hydrocephalus after 7 days of observation; identified as low risk for vasospasm or hydrocephalus. unstable neurosurgical patients requiring a lumbar drain for csf leak. patients with lumbar drains must stay in the icu. stable neurosurgical post-operative patients requiring frequent neuro monitoring. stable neurological patients at 24 hours; csf monitoring q2h or less frequent. unstable or new cervical spinal cord injury. stable spinal cord injury requiring neuro checks q2-3h. neuro checks, suctioning, and turning q4h or less frequent. acute neurologic disorders requiring nursing interventions q1h or more frequently. chronic but stable neurologic disorders (e.g., neuromuscular disease) requiring nursing interventions q2-3h. post-ictal patients slowly waking, protecting airway, needing ceeg and close neuro monitoring. 24-hour observation with nursing intervention q4h or less frequent.

records.title: step-down/pcu vs icu: admission criteria guide

records.title: appropriate for step-down / pcu (when clinically stable)
records.heading: appropriate for step-down / pcu (when clinically stable)
records.parentHeading: step-down/pcu vs icu: admission criteria guide
records.body: acute ischemic stroke requiring q2h neuro checks (e.g., icad or ica stenosis) who have remained stable after at least 24 hours of icu monitoring sah: no evd, stable or mildly elevated tcds, no change in neurologic baseline; requiring q2h neuro checks and/or close i/o monitoring during vasospasm surveillance ich: stable neuro exam, no continuous antihypertensive infusion, managed with prn iv antihypertensives and q2h neuro checks. escalate back to icu if frequent prn dosing or drip initiation becomes necessary. post-ictal: recurrent seizures resolved, airway protected; requiring close monitoring with ceeg and respiratory observation stable neuromuscular disease (e.g., mg, aidp) with adequate secretion management but requiring airway monitoring mma embolization with stable post-procedure course elective carotid or venous stent without hemodynamic instability stable post-operative or post-interventional neurosurgical patients (with nsgy/nil agreement) stable tracheostomy patients awaiting placement with minimal suction requirements

records.title: icu-level care required
records.heading: icu-level care required

records.title: part 9 · neurotrauma admission & icu management
records.heading: part 9 · neurotrauma admission & icu management
records.body: navigation cue: use this section for tbi, spine trauma, polytrauma, neuromonitoring, and service ownership. return to start here. tbi guide for akron - full details available on the teams channel. scenario admitting service critical care key points isolated mild-moderate tbi trauma service sicu neurosurgery consulted for neurosurgical management. isolated severe tbi trauma service (initial 24 h) neuroicu from admission sicu involvement not required. after 24 h, transfer to neurosurgery or neuroicu primary service; trauma signs off. spine trauma trauma service sicu consult neurosurgery or orthopedic spine surgery as appropriate. acute spinal cord injury trauma service (default) sicu workflow may evolve as advanced spinal cord monitoring is implemented; staff-to-staff discussion needed in such cases. polytrauma + severe tbi trauma service sicu + neuroicu co-manage severe tbi with significant extracranial injuries (thoracic, abdominal, pelvic, long-bone). nicu manages the tbi portion of critical care; neurosurgery consultation required. clear staff communication is essential.

records.title: neuromonitoring

records.body: patients requiring invasive neuromonitoring should, whenever possible, be admitted to the neuroicu (3200). if no neuroicu bed is available, or in selected high-injury-severity polytrauma cases, patients may be managed in one of the two neuromonitoring-capable beds on the 4th floor icu, at the discretion of the trauma team.

records.title: the clinical day and staff schedule
records.heading: the clinical day and staff schedule
records.body: source: nicu staff playbook 2026, sections 3-4. draft summary for orientation; confirm current expectations with nicu leadership. the clinical day (main campus). early daytime staff arrive at 6:30 am for sign-out in the nicu conference room per the long/short call delineation; night staff arrive at 6:30 pm. structured handoffs support early planning for extubations and step-down transfers. 8:30 am dispo rounds - multidisciplinary rounds in g20 with assistant nurse managers, case management, neurosurgery, and stroke to discuss dispositions, expedite transfers, and prepare planned admissions. 9:00 am bedside team rounds - systems-based and nurse-led; the responsible resident, fellow, and lip add assessment and plan. bedside teaching encouraged; aim to finish by noon. icu checklist - completed verbally and in epic at the end of rounds for every patient. 1:00 pm line/device huddle - review indwelling devices and ongoing necessity with anms and the team. a long call / short call model may be used, with short call leaving at 4:30 pm and the remaining staff member cross-covering both icus and consults. staff schedule. the goal is fair, equitable distribution of clinical coverage. qgenda is the official schedule and only up-to-date source of truth; spreadsheets are for viewing only. shift definitions: weekday am (mon-fri), weekend am (sat-sun), weekday pm (mon-wed), weekend pm (thu-sun). rest days are post-call days fully exempt from clinical and administrative duties. full-time ncc clinical commitment is 28 five-day weeks; partial fte is proportioned. scheduling is done in 6-month blocks (jan-jun, jul-dec) released at least 3 months in advance. recovery: one recovery day (monday) after a weekend shift; two recovery days (monday and tuesday) after a 7-day shift. night (pm) rotation: full-fte cv center providers complete two 6-week night rotations per year (2 weeks and 2 weekends each); adjusted for shared fte; opt-out available after age 55 in exchange for extra weekend shifts. holidays are distributed equally on a rotating basis (mid-year: memorial day, independence day, labor day; end-of-year: thanksgiving, christmas, new year's day). time away. off-service requests: up to two full weeks per semester, emailed to the unit director and schedule lead strictly before september 1 (jan-jun) and march 1 (jul-dec). holiday weeks and popular meeting weeks (ncs, sccm, aan) are excluded. vacation: requested only after the schedule is released, during non-clinical days; a call switch must be arranged first if during a clinical week. maximum contiguous vacation is 10 weekdays (14 days total); longer needs cv center director approval. 90 days' notice required. each provider has one well-being day and one floating holiday, requestable any time that does not interfere with clinical duties. meetings: ni funds one meeting per year; rank top 3 for the next calendar year by september 1. officers, committee members, and presenters get priority for their meeting. post-release changes: providers arrange their own call switches (except emergencies); changes are tracked but not counted toward fte. emergencies are escalated by phone/email to the unit director and schedule lead. the coordinator updates qgenda.

records.title: staff responsibilities
records.heading: staff responsibilities
records.body: source: nicu staff playbook 2026, section 5. draft summary; roles evolve with the new ni building and unit expansion. main campus clinical commitments. main campus nicu staff lead the clinical teams (fellows, residents, and apps) in the neurological icus. g20 staff supervise a 14-bed unit and team, generally with nicu fellow coverage, and complete death certificates during the week of service. h22 staff supervise a 10-bed unit and team, share pager triage with the on-service fellow, and (absent a consult attending) cover boarding patients in other icus and icu consults. future state: in the new ni building, coverage expands to three service attendings, each with 12-bed coverage and teams of fellows, apps, and residents. education, supervision, and documentation. attendings provide daily bedside education for residents, fellows, and apps, and discuss autonomy, expectations, and feedback with nicu fellows each week. procedural supervision is the attending's responsibility. all airway-related procedures require bedside, direct supervision by a nicu attending; rotating residents require direct supervision for any procedure. the attending is responsible for cosignature and billing of every patient in their icu (except app-covered patients on weekends and at ccf-akron general) and for verbal sign-out to the next physician. see the nicu staff orientation onboarding document for note and billing dot phrases. consult commitments. 8:30 am arrival for dispo rounds; coverage until 5 pm. the consult attending manages nicu boarders in other icus and icu consults (post-arrest neuroprognostication, cerebral edema, and status epilepticus), communicating with primary services and families. ccf-akron general nsicu commitments. in-house coverage 7 am - 5 pm (staff on site given airway responsibilities); home call during service weeks otherwise. dispo rounds at 8:45 am. weekend coverage begins 7 pm friday. see the separate akg nsicu playbook for details. nmet commitments: process pending; details to be added when finalized. administrative, research, and non-nicu responsibilities (didactics, committee participation, qi/ci, mortality review) are assigned by the section head and center director; records.body: source: article - death registration module in the new ohio vital records system set for go-live (ohio department of health, bureau of vital statistics). draft summary for awareness; verify the current workflow directly with the ohio department of health. ohio's electronic death registration system (edrs) is being replaced by the death registration module in the new ohio vital records system (ovrs), launching in phases in october-december 2025. e-physicians who certify deaths in edrs must migrate to the ovrs module after their phase go-live. phase i go-live wednesday, oct. 22 - coroners, e-physicians, and funeral home directors in 10 counties. phases ii-iv (nov. 19, dec. 1, dec. 15) - funeral home directors in additional counties. on the transition date, new death certificates cannot be started in edrs for counties going live; certificates already started in edrs continue there until completed and registered, then convert to ovrs. access to ovrs is only through ohio's secure ohid platform; create an ohid account at the ohid webpage. the new system adds enhanced security, mobile access, electronic submission, and integrated payment/ordering. questions: ovrs@odh.ohio.gov.

records.title: stroke discharge follow-up appointment order (epic)
records.heading: stroke discharge follow-up appointment order (epic)
records.body: source: epic change notice - hospital follow up appointment - neuro stroke (effective may 2026, all ohio locations only). draft summary; verify current order behavior in epic. what changed. the pm&r (physical medicine and rehabilitation) follow up appointment order is now preselected for all stroke patients when the neuro stroke follow up appointment order is used. previously, the pm&r order was preselected only if the patient was recommended for rehab services. open the neuro stroke follow-up appointment panel in the discharge follow up appointment orders. both the hospital follow up appointment - neuro stroke and hospital follow up appointment - physical medicine and rehabilitation orders populate (each 1 visit, qty-1, routine). the neuro stroke order schedules the follow-up within 7 days (home-going), 3-5 weeks (acute rehab), or 6-8 weeks (snf), with the cerebrovascular neuro center and readmission-risk prompts. the pm&r order captures the specific rehab service (e.g., stroke rehab, tbi, amputee, spasticity, cancer rehab, general rehab) and readmission-risk follow-up needs. florida locations will not have the pm&r follow up appointment order preselected with the neuro stroke order.

records.title: bleeding cvad: insertion to maintenance
records.heading: bleeding cvad: insertion to maintenance
records.body: source: 2026 adult inpatient bleeding cvad from insertion to maintenance algorithm (best practice; monica cummins, msn, aprn, accns-ag, pccn, clinical nurse specialist; algorithm march 2026). draft summary; follow product manufacturer instructions for use (mifu) and the clabsi resource site. a standardized approach to bleeding central venous access devices (cvad) reduces variation, misused products, and clabsi risk from frequent dressing changes, and improves cross-discipline collaboration. manual pressure is first, prior to any products. insertion: the procedure is not complete if the patient requires a pressure dressing for hemostasis or if bleeding persists. maintenance: apply products only as indicated and escalate for assistance if needed. use only products consistent with mifu. do not use surgicel on cvads. document products and interventions in the ehr. complex/coagulopathic bleeding: quikclot topical hemostatic 3.8 cm x 3.8 cm pre-slit (manufacturer number 188) may be used; do not put the slit under the catheter - place it on top to absorb bleeding. reference: adult inpatient cvad dressing troubleshooting guide and the clabsi line maintenance and handling resource. share with nursing, ip, physicians/lips, and sqpe.

records.title: multidisciplinary device surveillance rounding (mdsr)
records.heading: multidisciplinary device surveillance rounding (mdsr)
records.body: source: standardized multidisciplinary device surveillance rounding (mdsr) playbook (hai governance, version 1.0, 01.30.2026). draft summary; follow the current playbook and redcap tools on the infection prevention landing page. mdsr is a required, standardized, multidisciplinary rounding process for central lines and indwelling urinary catheters across cleveland clinic hospitals. rounds occur at least weekly to confirm insertion and maintenance bundle compliance, evaluate necessity, consider alternatives, and reduce cauti and clabsi. mdsr replaces prior collaborative rounds. team: provider/lip (physician or app), nursing leadership/quality, clinical nurse specialists, infection preventionists, and nursing quality representatives. central line assessment includes labeled/current tubing, blood-free connectors and lumens, correctly placed chg/algidex disc, clean/dry/dated dressing that is not overdue, a clear insertion site, and curos caps where appropriate. urinary catheter assessment includes documented peri/catheter care, intact seal and securement, no dependent loops, bag below bladder level and off the floor, and a bag that is not overfilled. lip review covers insertion checklist use, indication, line type/location, foley order and nurse driven foley removal (ndfr) order, duration, and keep/remove/replace decisions. number of devices to review weekly (by inpatient device volume): number of inpatient devices minimum required devices reviewed weekly 255 or more 20% of patients with devices 51 - 254 51 fewer than 51 no sampling: 100% of devices required data (cla, uca, and mdsr summaries) is entered in redcap the day rounds are completed for enterprise tracking. if an opportunity is found in more than 10% of rounds (goal 90% or higher compliance), implement targeted insertion, maintenance, or necessity interventions. removal considerations: remove central lines not used for more than 24 hours for central-access meds (48 hours for dialysis/apheresis), avoid lines for lab draws only, and remove urinary catheters when the original need is gone (external catheters can often measure output; consider bladder scans).

records.title: urinary retention in the acute care setting
records.heading: urinary retention in the acute care setting
records.body: source: urinary retention in the acute care setting / acute illness (physician/lip guidance, final 5-13-2026). draft summary for orientation; this is not a clinical protocol approval. confirm current guidance and consult urology as indicated. acute urinary retention is the sudden inability to voluntarily pass urine (possibly with suprapubic pain, bloating, or urgency). chronic retention is a post-void residual (pvr) greater than 300 ml persisting at least 6 months on two separate occasions. initial assessment considerations. evaluate precipitating medications (anticholinergics, alpha-adrenergic agonists, calcium channel blockers, opioids, benzodiazepines, muscle relaxants) and consider holding contributors. assess comorbidities (bph, spinal cord injury, fecal impaction, chronic constipation, diabetic neuropathy, neurologic illness, deconditioning), perform a focused exam, and review labs (glucose, hgba1c, urinalysis with reflex culture) and imaging. consider a urology consult to facilitate the plan of care. determine etiology: obstructive, infectious, post-operative, or neurologic/medical. neurologic/medical: intermittent catheterization (ic) is first-line; evaluate glucose/hgba1c for neurogenic bladder; bladder scan to monitor pvr. if ic volume is under 500 ml, next ic in 6 hours; if not, next ic in 4 hours. obstructive (bph, fecal impaction/constipation, urethral stricture, or post-operative): treat the cause; for bph start/resume an alpha-blocker at insertion and maintain the indwelling catheter at least 3 days before a trial of void (tov). infectious: obtain diagnostic imaging and urinalysis with reflex culture; consider urology consult. a tov is successful when the patient voids with pvr 150-400 ml and no retention symptoms; if unsuccessful, resume catheterization and arrange urology follow-up. key terms: iuc (indwelling urinary catheter), ic (intermittent catheterization), tov (trial of void), pvr (post-void residual). interpret bladder scans cautiously with ascites, obesity, or anasarca, and defer catheter placement to urology for special cases (e.g., artificial urinary sphincter, recent urethroplasty/prostatectomy).

records.title: heparin anti-xa nomogram updates
records.heading: heparin anti-xa nomogram updates
records.body: source: lip heparin nomogram updates presentation (july 2026; enterprise anticoagulation committee and pharmacy & therapeutics). draft summary; verify current order sets, ranges, and eligibility in epic. questions: anticoagstewardship@ccf.org. heparin anti-xa nomograms became available july 7, 2026 as the standard of practice for iv heparin monitoring. excluded locations: ohio region (ashtabula regional medical center, union hospital, and all freestanding eds) and florida region (indian river and the martin health system). rationale: faster time to therapeutic, more consistent levels unaffected by acute-phase reactants, lupus anticoagulant, or factor deficiencies, and fewer lab draws. standard target is 0.3-0.7 units/ml for most indications. limitations: the assay is affected by oral factor xa inhibitors (apixaban, edoxaban, rivaroxaban), low-molecular-weight heparin, and fondaparinux. patients exposed to doacs or parenteral xa inhibitors within 5 days are monitored by aptt. the order set prompts anti-xa eligibility screening (outpatient factor xa inhibitor history in the past 180 days; inpatient administrations in the past 5 days) and standardized baseline labs and monitoring; there is no change to nomogram order structure or dosing. updated nomenclature: current updated med heparin standard (dvt/pe) - nomogram standard intensity nomogram med heparin low dose/acs - nomogram lower intensity nomogram med heparin stroke nomogram no bolus lower intensity nomogram therapeutic range changes: nomogram parameter old range new range standard intensity aptt 53-78 seconds no change standard intensity heparin anti-xa level 0.3-0.7 units/ml no change lower intensity / no bolus lower intensity aptt 49-67 seconds 53-67 seconds lower intensity / no bolus lower intensity heparin anti-xa level 0.2-0.5 units/ml 0.3-0.5 units/ml ancillary alignment: calculators display when the next aptt and anti-xa labs are due; notify-physician conditions and nursing instructions were standardized (e.g., no im injections retained; gastroccult-all-emesis and emar rate logging removed).

records.title: donation after circulatory death (dcd) workflow
records.heading: donation after circulatory death (dcd) workflow
records.parentHeading: part 8 · end-of-life care, organ donation & dnc
records.body: source: dcd (donation after circulatory determination of death) workflow. draft summary for orientation; organ donation is coordinated by lifebanc and this page requires named clinical review before operational use. references include the hrsa dcd directives (january 2026) and the ast-asts joint statement on dcd (2025 update). referral and independence. lifebanc is notified prior to dnr-cc withdrawal of life-sustaining support; the primary team confirms the withdrawal decision independent of donation. hospital management (before or). confirm withdrawal remains clinically appropriate (reassess q12h and within 2h of withdrawal); obtain and scan legal authorization for dcd into the emr; consult palliative/hospice if needed. the primary team maintains medical management until death; lifebanc does not write pre-pronouncement orders. code status (dnr-cca vs organ-preservation) and consent for procedures/anticoagulants and nrp use are clarified with the family and lifebanc. a multidisciplinary pre-or huddle (lifebanc, icu nurse, staff physician, and the independent accompanying physician who will pronounce) is completed; an arterial line is working (upper-extremity if nrp thoracic recovery), and a reintubation plan and disposition plan (if death does not occur) are established. operating room management. or huddle confirms code status and comfort measures; the surgical team exits prior to withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy (wlst); heparin is administered per consent; extubation and discontinuation of mechanical/pharmacologic support are performed. after zero pulse pressure on the arterial line (or absent doppler flow) and cessation of respiration, a 5-minute observation with continuous zero pulse pressure and strict no-touch conditions is maintained; the period restarts if any cardiac impulse or doppler activity is detected. death is pronounced and documented by the accompanying physician; the organ recovery team enters only after pronouncement. late autoresuscitation during procurement requires stopping, repeating the 5-minute asystole confirmation with no-touch, and communicating with the opo and surgical team before restarting. if death does not occur, the patient is transferred to an appropriate bed and comfort measures continue.

records.title: determination of death by neurologic criteria (dnc) in adults
records.heading: determination of death by neurologic criteria (dnc) in adults
records.parentHeading: part 8 · end-of-life care, organ donation & dnc
records.body: source: dnc flow chart procedure (v2). draft summary for orientation; determination of death by neurologic criteria (dnc / brain death) requires dnc mylearning course completion and named clinical review before operational use. references include the world brain death project (jama 2020) and the aan 2023 consensus guideline. prerequisites (all must be met). dnc mylearning course completed; printed dnc procedure at the bedside. coma is irreversible and the cause is known, with neuroimaging compatible with the clinical findings (catastrophic supratentorial injury; posterior fossa injury must show a compatible catastrophic picture). cns depressant drug effect absent (e.g., pentobarbital serum level under 5 mcg/ml, ethanol under 80 mg/dl; wait 5 or more elimination half-lives when levels cannot be measured); no residual paralytics; no severe acid-base, electrolyte, or endocrine abnormality. normothermia (core temperature above 36 c for more than 24 hours); sbp at least 100 mmhg and map above 75 mmhg (vasopressors permitted); no spontaneous respirations. contact lifebanc and the end-of-life care team as needed. clinical examination (exam 1 and exam 2; all findings must be present on each exam). pupils mid-size to dilated (3 mm or larger), non-reactive to bright light; corneal reflex absent; oculocephalic reflex absent (only if c-spine integrity ensured) and oculovestibular reflex absent. no facial movement to noxious stimuli at the supraorbital nerve or temporomandibular joint; gag reflex absent; cough reflex absent to tracheal suctioning; no motor response to noxious stimuli in all four limbs (spinally mediated reflexes are permissible). if the oculocephalic reflex cannot be assessed due to cervical spine or skull-base concerns, dnc can still be determined without ancillary testing if oculovestibular reflexes are absent bilaterally. apnea testing and ancillary testing. apnea testing follows once prerequisites are met (see the apnea testing procedure page). a positive test is an arterial ph under 7.30 with paco2 of 60 mmhg or higher and at least 20 mmhg above baseline. ancillary testing (tcd, cerebral angiogram, or nuclear scintigraphy cerebral blood-flow study) is required when the clinical exam or apnea test cannot be completed or interpreted with certainty, or when confounders cannot be resolved; for ventricular assist devices or aortic balloon pump, consider cerebral angiogram or nuclear scintigraphy. ancillary testing is not a substitute for a complete clinical brain death examination. time of death is the time arterial ph and paco2 reached the target value reported in the record; when apnea or the clinical exam cannot be fully performed, it is when the ancillary test is officially reported.

records.title: apnea testing procedure (ventilated and ecmo)
records.heading: apnea testing procedure (ventilated and ecmo)
records.parentHeading: determination of death by neurologic criteria (dnc) in adults
records.body: source: dnc flow chart procedure (v2), apnea testing. draft summary; requires dnc training and named clinical review before use. reference: bein & citerio, intensive care med 2019 (brain death under extracorporeal life support). apnea test in ventilated patients. patient is hemodynamically stable (vasopressors may keep sbp above 100 mmhg and map above 75) with no major electrolyte, acid-base, or metabolic derangement. adjust the ventilator to normocarbia (paco2 35-45 mmhg) and ph 7.35-7.45 (unless a co2 retainer); pre-oxygenate with 100% fio2 for more than 10 minutes. disconnect the ventilator and provide oxygen via extension tubing near the carina at 6 l/min; spontaneous respirations should be absent. draw arterial blood gas at 5-7 minutes and every 5 minutes until the goal paco2 is reached, then reconnect the ventilator. a positive test is ph under 7.30 with paco2 of 60 mmhg or higher and at least 20 mmhg above baseline, with absent respiration. abort for sbp under 100 or map under 75 despite support, oxygen saturation below 85%, or a cardiac arrhythmia with hemodynamic instability. if normal ph/paco2 cannot be maintained, ancillary testing is mandatory in addition to apnea testing. apnea test on ecmo. coordinate with the primary icu team. adjust the ecmo sweep and/or ventilator to physiologic ph and eucapnia (paco2 35-45 mmhg); for va or hybrid ecmo use right upper-extremity arterial and post-oxygenator gases, and for vv ecmo any arterial line is sufficient. keep the oxygenator fdo2 at 100%; disconnect the ventilator and oxygenate via a cannula at the carina at 6-9 l/min; gradually reduce the gas sweep to as low as 0.5 l/min as tolerated; watch for any respiratory movement including a brief gasp. repeat abgs after 5-10 minutes and every 5 minutes until the goal paco2 is reached while the patient remains stable; the same positive-test threshold and abort criteria apply, reinitiating ecmo on the prior settings if aborted.
